blocks.text: Phenylamine gives two types of reactions:

blocks.alt: Phenylamine drawn with a Kekule benzene ring joined to an N atom carrying a lone pair and two H atoms. Arrows from a line labelled sp2 hybridized point up to the ring carbons; an arrow from sp2 hybridized points up to the N.
blocks.caption: Hybridisation in phenylamine: sp2 ring carbons and the nitrogen atom (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 124).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book labels the nitrogen of phenylamine sp³ hybridized, but on the page before (Figure 24.1) it says the nitrogen is planar, with its lone pair in a p orbital that overlaps the ring; that is sp², as drawn above. (In real phenylamine the nitrogen is slightly pyramidal, between sp² and sp³.)

The amino group (–NH₂) is an ortho-para directing group. Therefore, the incoming electrophile attacks at “o” and “p” positions. The presence of the amino group makes benzene ring fairly reactive, especially at these position. Hence, bromination of phenylamine is faster than benzene, and its two ortho and the para positions, all are occupied in a single reaction.

blocks.alt: Phenylamine (ring with NH2) + 3Br2 gives 2,4,6-tribromophenylamine (white precipitate), a ring with NH2 at the top and Br at the two ortho positions and the para position, + 3HBr.
blocks.caption: Bromination of phenylamine to 2,4,6-tribromophenylamine (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 125).

blocks.text: b) Reaction with Nitrous Acid and Formation of Azo Compounds

Phenylamine being a primary amine reacts with nitrous acid to form phenyldiazonium salt. This reaction is called diazotization. The organic compounds having diazonium ion, –N⁺≡N (diazo group) as a functional group are called diazo compounds. Both aliphatic and aromatic primary amines react with nitrous acid to yield diazonium salts. Nitrous acid is unstable and is prepared in situ by the reaction of sodium nitrite and HCl. The reaction mixture is kept below 10 °C using ice. This is because the diazonium salts are unstable and will decompose easily, giving off nitrogen gas, N₂, even at room temperature.

blocks.alt: Three lines: NaNO2 + HCl gives HNO2 + NaCl; phenylamine + HNO2 + HCl, less than 10 degrees C, gives phenyldiazonium chloride (ring-N(+) triple bond N Cl-) + 2H2O; phenyldiazonium chloride + H2O, Heat, gives phenol + N2 + HCl.
blocks.caption: Diazotisation of phenylamine and hydrolysis of phenyldiazonium chloride to phenol (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 125).

blocks.text: The alkyl diazonium salts are highly unstable under all conditions and therefore cannot be isolated. The aryl diazonium salts are however fairly stable at low temperatures. The extra stability of aromatic diazo compounds compared to aliphatic diazo compounds is due to the delocalization of the positive charge over the aromatic ring. Benzene diazonium salts are the important intermediates in the synthesis of many organic compounds.

blocks.alt: A Kekule benzene ring joined to N(+) triple bond N, with the + on the nitrogen attached to the ring.
blocks.caption: Structure of benzene diazonium ion (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 125).

blocks.text: The reactions of aryl diazonium salts with strongly activated aromatic compounds, such as phenols and amines, are called coupling reactions. The products of such reactions containing a –N=N– bond are called azo compounds. In the coupling reaction, the positively charged diazonium ion acts as an electrophile. It substitutes into the benzene ring of phenol at the para position.
Coupling with phenol occurs in mild alkaline solution and with aromatic amines in mild acidic conditions.

blocks.alt: Over two lines: benzenediazonium chloride (ring-N(+) triple bond N Cl-) + phenol (ring-OH), with NaOH over the arrow, gives p-hydroxyazobenzene (orange solid), ring-N=N-ring-OH.
blocks.caption: Coupling of benzenediazonium chloride with phenol (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 126).

blocks.alt: Mechanism: Ph-N=N(+) + phenol (Kekule ring) with curly arrows from the O lone pair and the ring pi bonds to the terminal N; the intermediate Ph-N=N-C(H) ring with C=O(+)H and curly arrows from the C-H bond into the ring and from the C=O bond onto O; then, with loss of H+, p-hydroxyazobenzene (an azo compound).
blocks.caption: Mechanism of the coupling of the diazonium ion with phenol (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 126).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The last step of the printed mechanism shows ‘–H’; a proton is lost, –H⁺, as drawn above.

Coupling reaction can be used to form different types of azo dyes. p-Dimethylaminoazo benzene is called Butter yellow, which was previously used in food. However, due to its carcinogenic nature, its use in food is now forbidden.

blocks.alt: Over two lines: benzenediazonium chloride (Kekule ring) + N,N-dimethylphenylamine (ring-N(CH3)2), with CH3COOH over the arrow, gives p-dimethylaminoazo benzene (butter yellow), ring-N=N-ring-N(CH3)2, + HCl.
blocks.caption: Formation of butter yellow (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 126).

blocks.text: Methyl orange is an acid-base indicator and is prepared from diazotized sulfanilic acid and N, N-diamethylphenylamine as follows.

blocks.alt: Over two lines: NaO3S-ring-N(+) triple bond N Cl- (diazotised sulphanilic acid) + N,N-dimethylphenylamine, with CH3COOH over the arrow, gives methyl orange, NaO3S-ring-N=N-ring-N(CH3)2, + HCl.
blocks.caption: Formation of methyl orange (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 126).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed scheme draws the product with N triple bond N and gives it the name of butter yellow (p-dimethylaminoazo benzene); the azo group is N=N and the product is methyl orange, as drawn above.

The azo group (Ph-N=N-Ph) in azo dyes is called a chromophore. This group is responsible for the intense colour of the dyes ranging from yellow and orange to red, blue and green depending upon what other groups are attached to the benzene rings.
Azo dyes are the coloured compounds which are prepared by the reaction of diazonium salt of phenylamine and some aryl compound having activated benzene ring.
